title: The Newest Reading or All of Them: Acting on the Past

questions.question: A 500 Hz device is read by a 100 Hz loop that takes one message per tick. What happens to the queue?
options: It stays empty because the loop is fast enough
It grows to the size of the driver's buffer and stays there, so the loop acts on old data
The device slows down to match
The oldest messages are dropped automatically
questions.explanation: Each tick removes one and the device adds five. Nothing tells the device to slow down, and nothing reports the growth.

questions.question: The loop acted on data 3741 ms old at worst. Where does that number come from?
options: A bug in the timestamps
4096 bytes is 372 frames, and 372 frames drained at 100 a second takes 3.72 seconds
The device's clock drifts
The checksum takes time to compute
questions.explanation: The full buffer keeps what it holds, so the head of the queue is 372 frames deep and the loop drains it at its own rate.

questions.question: Handling every waiting message, at 3 ms each in a 10 ms tick, still fell behind. Why?
options: It handled 300 a second against 500 sent, so it fell behind more slowly
Handling every message is always wrong
The buffer is too small
The ticks were not regular
questions.explanation: Mean age fell from 2472 ms to 962 ms and the worst case to 1245 ms, which is 372 frames at 300 a second. Better and not fixed.

questions.question: Why does drain_latest take a limit?
options: To save memory
A device that sends as fast as the loop reads means nothing is ever waiting, so an unbounded drain never returns and the loop misses its deadline
Links cannot hold more than 64 messages
To make the function faster
questions.explanation: The loop has a deadline and a call that lasts as long as the device chooses cannot be inside it. The `more` flag says it stopped at the limit.

questions.question: A loop integrates encoder increments using the newest of each drain, and the distance comes out 99 percent short. What kind of message is an increment?
options: A state, so the newest is enough
A change, so each one has to be added and a skipped one is lost; carrying a running total would turn it into a state
Neither
It depends on the baud rate
questions.explanation: The newest is a policy for states. For changes the sum is what matters, and 990 of 1000 was thrown away unused.

questions.question: The newest message is copied out of the link instead of being kept as a view. Why?
options: Views are slow
The link's message is only valid until the next poll, and the drain polls again before it returns
The checksum would fail
The message is encrypted
questions.explanation: A view kept across a poll points at bytes the link has already overwritten. The copy must also check its size, or a large message writes past the destination.
